originalGroup.material:
Planning a campus soup stall

When students opened a lunch stall for a campus festival, their first difficulty was deciding how much soup to make. They began with an ____1____ of the number of visitors, based on advance ticket sales. It was useful as a starting point, but it could not tell them exactly how many people would want lunch.

The team wanted to avoid food ____2____ without disappointing hungry customers. On the first day, ____3____ was strongest just after a morning lecture ended. The students sold nearly all their soup within twenty minutes, then waited through a quiet afternoon.

For the second day, they counted the number of ____4____ served during each half-hour period. They kept unused ____5____, such as dry lentils and unopened spices, apart from food that had already been cooked. This made it easier to see what could safely remain in stock for another day.

The new information helped them ____6____ their preparation times. It also showed that extra ____7____ were needed: several customers wanted to take soup to their friends rather than eat beside the stall.

The team posted a sign showing which soups were still ____8____ for purchase. They did not promise that every flavour would last until closing time. Instead, they kept the menu ____9____, changing it at short notice according to the supplies on hand.

After the festival, unused clean bowls were ____10____ to the supplier. The students had learned that a good plan was not simply a large quantity prepared in advance. It was a set of decisions that could respond to what happened during the day.

originalGroup.material:
Sharing a limited printing service

A university design workshop had three printers capable of producing large three-dimensional models. As more departments began to use them, the ____1____ of printing time became contentious. A single overnight job could delay several small projects, while a rule favouring short jobs could make ambitious models almost impossible to complete.

The coordinator began by listing the service's practical ____2____: machine capacity, staff hours and the time required to prepare each material. These limits could not be removed by asking users to cooperate more enthusiastically. Once they were visible, however, the discussion could focus on choices within them.

Printing slots were then ____3____ across departments according to a published trial schedule. Users were given modest ____4____ to release unused reservations early: doing so allowed them priority when requesting a later slot. Participation in the trial was ____5____, rather than a condition imposed on every department, so the coordinator was careful not to describe its users as representative of the whole university.

The schedule could not ____6____ every competing preference. Instead, the coordinator recorded which kinds of request were repeatedly postponed. The rules remained ____7____ during the first term, explicitly open to revision once the team understood their effects. Publishing both the rules and the reasons for exceptions made the process more ____8____ to users who had previously seen only an unexplained refusal.

One department proposed removing every spare interval from the schedule. Another argued that some ____9____ was needed so a machine failure would not disrupt all later work. The final plan retained a limited buffer, whose use would be reviewed rather than assumed to be permanently necessary.

The workshop also ____10____ records of the original requests, not merely the eventual bookings. Otherwise, a successful-looking schedule might conceal the projects that had never secured a place. The trial did not settle the argument about fairness. It gave that argument a more specific set of decisions to examine.

originalGroup.material:
Making a route guide useful

When our walking club redesigned its route guide, the editor began with a question about ____1____ (RELY). Could readers trust a short description to help them choose a suitable walk? A cheerful phrase such as "an easy morning" gave little information about steps or uneven ground.

The group invited a visitor to comment on the route's ____2____ (ACCESS). Her questions revealed several ____3____ (ASSUME) that regular walkers had never written down. They knew where the steep section began and where a gate opened, but newcomers did not.

To make a useful ____4____ (COMPARE) between routes, we replaced broad labels with specific distances and surface descriptions. The ____5____ (ACCURATE) of those details mattered more than giving every walk an equally attractive title.

Some obstacles had previously been almost ____6____ (VISIBLE) in our descriptions: they were never mentioned, even though they affected people's choices. A brief ____7____ (EXPLAIN) beside each route now identified its known limitations and the date of the latest check.

The editor retained final ____8____ (RESPONSIBLE) for publishing the guide, but asked members to report changes. No description could make the route suitable for everyone. It could, however, make the choice better informed.
